item.description:
A day now ends when your day ends

The figures under "Usage on this Mac" were grouped into UTC days while everything above them said "today" and named a weekday. Two hours east of Greenwich that meant a day began at 02:00 on your clock, and everything you did between midnight and 02:00 was filed under yesterday.

On the machine this was found on, a morning that had cost 288 million tokens read as 120 million. Nothing was ever lost — the tokens sat in the previous day — but no number labelled "today" was the day you were living through.

Days are now cut on your own clock, everywhere: the daily chart, the spend tile, "last 7 days" and "last 30 days", and the name under a selected bar.

Your figures change with this update

Which way depends on when you work.

  • Today usually goes up, by whatever you did between midnight and the old boundary.
  • Individual days shift by a few hours' worth of work in either direction as their boundaries move.
  • Two days may drop sharply. On the reference machine, two days were still carrying the double counting that 1.5 corrected everywhere else — they could not be corrected then, and can be now. See below.
  • If your Mac is set to UTC, nothing about your figures changes at all. The old grid and the new one are the same grid.

Why two days could not be corrected before, and can be now

1.5 corrected a day only when the transcripts still on disk accounted for what had been recorded for it — otherwise files had gone missing and the recorded figure was the better evidence. That test is unchanged and still protects days whose transcripts are gone.

What has changed is what it is measured against. It now compares against figures 1.5 already corrected, so a day whose files are all still there clears the test comfortably where it used to sit just under the line. Days with genuinely missing transcripts keep their recorded figures, exactly as before.

What this does to what was already recorded

Correcting the grid only fixes new readings, so this update also re-reads the transcripts once and re-cuts the recorded days on your clock. It happens in the background on the first launch after updating, and needs no window open.

If your history reaches back to days whose transcripts no longer exist, those days keep the figures they have. They are the reason a total over "All Time" can still read higher than a fresh count of the transcripts would: it includes usage that was really recorded and can no longer be recounted.

Requires macOS 26.

Corrections to 1.5

Two figures 1.5 got wrong, and both are visible.

Local usage stopped updating

1.5 moved Glyphline into the menu bar, and the reading of ~/.claude/projects was still wired to the dashboard window — which that release stopped opening at launch. So on a machine where the dashboard was never opened, "Usage on this Mac" never updated at all; and where it was opened, it was read once and then not again for as long as the app kept running.

The reading now happens on its own, at launch and then on the same interval as the account sync, whether or not a window is open. It also re-reads when the Mac wakes, instead of waiting out an interval that elapsed while it slept.

It is deliberately not tied to the "Sync automatically" switch: that switch is about network calls to your provider, and reading files on this Mac costs nothing outside it.

The Agentverse showed every agent at about twice its size

The per-session token totals behind the Agentverse carried the same double counting 1.5 fixed for the daily figures — the same assistant message counted once per transcript that contained it. 1.5 corrected the daily numbers and left these alone.

They are corrected once now, on the first launch after updating, by the same rule: a session is recalculated only when the transcripts still on disk account for what was recorded for it. Where transcripts have gone — Claude Code used to keep subagent sessions in separate files and now records them inline — the recorded figure is left exactly as it was, rather than dropping to a partial view of itself.

Requires macOS 26.

Glyphline now lives in the menu bar

After this update Glyphline starts into the menu bar. No window opens, and there is no Dock icon — the icon appears only while the dashboard or the Agentverse is actually open, and goes away again when you close it.

Nothing is missing. The dashboard is one click away in the menu bar panel, and it can be open as long as you like. If you would rather have the old behaviour — a window at launch and a permanent Dock icon — choose Window under App Mode in Settings.

The App Mode setting has two options now instead of three. The one that was removed only decided whether the window opened by itself at launch, which is exactly what separates the two that remain.

Quota cards say when a window comes back

A card reading 0% free now tells you when it resets, as both a wait and a clock time — "resets in 2d 4h (Thu 14:00)". The menu bar panel and the accounts list already carried the countdown; the cards were the one place that stayed silent about the only question a spent window raises.

Your local usage numbers change with this update

They go down, and on a heavy machine they can roughly halve. That is the fix, not a regression — the old figures were too high.

What was wrong

Glyphline reads the Claude Code transcripts under ~/.claude/projects. Claude Code copies a session's history into a new file whenever the session is resumed or forked, so the same assistant message — same id, same usage block — sits in several files at once. The scanner summed the files line by line, which counted every one of those copies. On the machine this was measured on it recorded 2.19× the real usage: 45.5 Gtok against 20.4 Gtok.

Every message is now counted once, by its id.

What this update does to what was already recorded

Fixing the scanner only fixes new readings, so this update also corrects the history once, on the first launch after updating. It happens in the background and needs no window open.

It does not simply throw the history away and read everything again, because that would lose real usage. Transcripts disappear: Claude Code used to write subagent sessions into their own files and now records them inline, and sessions run in git worktrees that were later removed leave nothing behind at all. On the reference machine 11.5 Gtok of genuinely recorded usage had no source left to read, and two days had no surviving transcript whatsoever.

So each day is decided on evidence. If the transcripts still on disk account for what was recorded for that day, the corrected figure replaces it. If they fall short, files are missing, and the recorded figure is left exactly as it was.

Fixes

  • Renaming an account now reaches the dashboard cards and the menu bar straight away. It used to show up only after the next sync or a restart.
  • The menu bar panel closes when you open the dashboard or the Agentverse from it, instead of staying open over the window it just raised.

Requires macOS 26.

A calmer menu bar

Three things the app was doing that it did not need to do.

The panel no longer rescrapes the web every time you open it

Reading a quota means loading an account's page in a web view and running a script against the rendered document — a real browser navigation, per account. The menu bar panel asked for one every time it opened, so with three accounts that was three page renders per click, on the thread that draws the panel you are standing in.

There is now a sixty second floor, far below the rate a five-hour or weekly window can move, and a scheduled refresh counts towards it.

It no longer re-asserts its activation policy on every open

Opening the panel re-set the app's activation policy even when it already was what the setting asked for. That turns a no-op into a real state change: macOS re-evaluates app activation underneath a panel that is in the middle of opening, which can make it flicker, close, or come back twice — and it is worse with more than one display.

The Agentverse stops drawing frames it cannot tell apart

The scene is computed from a frame counter that advances 60 times a second, but the animation ran at the display's refresh rate. On a 120 Hz screen every other frame rebuilt the entire scene and rasterised it to produce a picture identical to the one already on screen.

Measured at the window's real size, the datastream view costs 6.2 ms a frame with six sessions against an 8.3 ms budget at 120 Hz — so the half being discarded was the half that made it stutter.

Also

This update window now shows these notes rather than the GitHub page they used to be linked to, which arrived complete with header, navigation and a sign-in button in a 500 point wide frame.

Requires macOS 26.
